title: Grade 9 Science — Diversity in Living Organisms
description: Classification of living organisms — Five Kingdoms, hierarchy, plant/animal groups (CBSE Ch. 7)
subject: science

questions.question: The basis of classification of living organisms includes:
options: Only body colour and habitat
Cell structure, mode of nutrition, body organisation, and phylogenetic relationships
Only the presence or absence of a nucleus
Only the number of legs and body segments
questions.explanation: Classification is based on multiple criteria: cell structure (prokaryote/eukaryote), mode of nutrition (autotrophic/heterotrophic), body organisation, and evolutionary relationships (phylogeny).

questions.question: The Five Kingdom classification of living organisms was proposed by:
options: Carl Linnaeus
Charles Darwin
R.H. Whittaker
Ernst Haeckel
questions.explanation: R.H. Whittaker (1969) proposed the Five Kingdom classification: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia. Carl Linnaeus proposed the two-kingdom classification (Plants and Animals).

questions.question: Kingdom Monera includes organisms that are:
options: Unicellular eukaryotes with a defined nucleus
Multicellular organisms with cell walls
Prokaryotes — no nuclear membrane, no membrane-bound organelles
Organisms that perform photosynthesis only
questions.explanation: Monera (bacteria, blue-green algae/cyanobacteria) are prokaryotes — their genetic material is not enclosed within a nuclear membrane, and they lack membrane-bound organelles.

questions.question: Amoeba and Paramecium belong to Kingdom:
options: Monera
Fungi
Plantae
Protista
questions.explanation: Kingdom Protista includes unicellular eukaryotes (cells have a defined nucleus). Amoeba (pseudopod locomotion) and Paramecium (cilia locomotion) are classic examples of Protista.

questions.question: Which feature distinguishes Fungi from Plants?
options: Fungi are unicellular; plants are multicellular
Fungi are eukaryotes; plants are prokaryotes
Fungi have chitin cell walls and are heterotrophic; plants have cellulose cell walls and are autotrophic
Fungi live in water; plants live on land
questions.explanation: Fungi have cell walls made of chitin and obtain nutrition by decomposing dead organic matter (saprophytic/heterotrophic). Plants have cellulose cell walls and manufacture food through photosynthesis (autotrophic).

questions.question: Binomial nomenclature — the system of giving each organism a two-part scientific name — was introduced by:
options: Charles Darwin
Carl Linnaeus
R.H. Whittaker
Gregor Mendel
questions.explanation: Carl Linnaeus introduced binomial nomenclature in Systema Naturae (1758). Each organism gets a genus name + species name (e.g., Homo sapiens). Names are in Latin/Greek and written in italics.

questions.question: The correct hierarchy of classification from broadest to most specific is:
options: Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species
Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum → Kingdom
Kingdom → Class → Phylum → Family → Order → Genus → Species
Phylum → Kingdom → Class → Family → Order → Genus → Species
questions.explanation: The taxonomic hierarchy from broadest to most specific: Kingdom → Phylum → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species. A helpful mnemonic: 'King Philip Came Over For Great Soup.'

questions.question: Thallophyta (Division of Plantae) includes:
options: Mosses and liverworts
Ferns and horsetails
Algae — simple plants with no true roots, stems, or leaves
Gymnosperms like pine and Cycas
questions.explanation: Thallophyta are the simplest plants — algae (Spirogyra, Ulva, Fucus). Their body is a thallus (not differentiated into roots, stems, leaves). They are mostly aquatic.

questions.question: Bryophyta are called the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom' because:
options: They can live on both land and in water
They have both roots and leaves
They reproduce only in water but live on land
They have both autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition
questions.explanation: Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts — e.g., Funaria, Marchantia) need water for reproduction (flagellated sperm must swim to reach eggs) but live on land. This dual dependency earns them the title 'amphibians of the plant kingdom.'

questions.question: Pteridophyta are significant in plant evolution because they are:
options: The first land plants with no vascular tissue
The first plants with seeds
The first plants with vascular tissue (xylem and phloem) but no seeds
The first flowering plants
questions.explanation: Pteridophytes (ferns, Selaginella, horsetails) were the first plants to develop vascular tissue (xylem for water/minerals, phloem for food) — enabling taller body structures. However, they still reproduce via spores, not seeds.

questions.question: Gymnosperms (e.g., pine, Cycas, deodar) are characterised by:
options: Seeds enclosed inside a fruit
No seeds — reproduction only by spores
Naked seeds — not enclosed in a fruit (ovary wall absent)
Seeds enclosed in a hard shell but no leaves
questions.explanation: 'Gymno' = naked, 'sperma' = seed. Gymnosperms bear naked seeds on the surface of cone scales, with no fruit wall (ovary) surrounding them. Examples: Pinus (pine), Cycas, Cedrus (deodar).

questions.question: Porifera (e.g., sponges) are the simplest animals because:
options: They are unicellular
They have a porous body with no true tissues or organs
They can photosynthesise
They have a hard exoskeleton
questions.explanation: Porifera (sponges) have bodies full of pores (osculum, ostia) through which water circulates. They lack true tissues, organs, or organ systems — making them the simplest multicellular animals.

questions.question: Amphibians (e.g., frog, salamander, toad) are characterised by:
options: Warm-blooded, four-chambered heart, lay eggs on land
Cold-blooded, can live on land and in water, lay eggs in water
Cold-blooded, only aquatic, breathe through gills throughout life
Warm-blooded, bear live young ones, nurse with milk
questions.explanation: Amphibians are cold-blooded (ectothermic) vertebrates that can live on land and in water. They breathe through gills as larvae and lungs/skin as adults. They lay eggs in water (no amniotic egg).

questions.question: What distinguishes mammals from all other vertebrates?
options: They are warm-blooded
They have a four-chambered heart
They have hair/fur on their body and nurse young ones with milk from mammary glands
They breathe through lungs
questions.explanation: The defining characteristics of mammals are: (1) presence of hair/fur, and (2) mammary glands for suckling young ones. They are also warm-blooded and most give birth to live young, but the defining traits are hair and milk production.

questions.question: Angiosperms differ from Gymnosperms in that Angiosperms have:
options: Vascular tissue (xylem and phloem)
Seeds enclosed within a fruit (ovary wall develops into fruit)
Naked seeds with no protective covering
No flowers — they reproduce by spores
questions.explanation: 'Angio' = enclosed, 'sperma' = seed. In Angiosperms (flowering plants), seeds are enclosed within a fruit formed from the ovary wall after fertilisation. They are the most evolved and diverse plant group.
